name: Retinyl acetate
lead: Retinyl acetate (vitamin A acetate) is a synthetic, fat-soluble ester of retinol. It is used to fortify foods such as margarine, plant-based milks and cereals, appears in multivitamins, and is included in some anti-aging skincare products, where it is presented as a more stable, gentler alternative to retinol [1].

After ingestion it is hydrolyzed in the intestine to retinol, which is re-esterified and stored mainly as retinyl palmitate in the liver [1]. No published human trial of topical retinyl acetate for appearance was found.

paras: The acetyl group protects the alcohol end of retinol, making the compound more resistant than free retinol to heat, oxygen and light, though its polyene chain remains sensitive, so formulators add antioxidants such as tocopherol and use opaque packaging [1].

Retinyl acetate is converted to retinol, which can be oxidized to retinoic acid, the active signaling form. Laboratory studies in the 1970s and 1980s examined retinyl acetate and vitamin A effects on epidermal cell differentiation, including mouse epidermal cells and cultured human keratinocytes [3][2]. Studies measured binding of retinol and related compounds to retinol-binding proteins [4].

No studies found of retinyl acetate as a topical appearance treatment. A series of registered phase I and II trials used QLT091001, a retinoid formulation, orally in inherited retinal disease and impaired dark adaptation [5][6][7]; these concern vision, not skin.

Retinyl acetate carries the dose-dependent risks of other vitamin A forms, including hypervitaminosis A; phototoxicity is reported to be lower than retinol but can occur in formulations lacking UV stabilizers [1]. The EU's SCCS considers leave-on cosmetics safe up to 0.3% retinol equivalents, with a 0.05% ceiling suggested for body lotions for ages 1 to 3 [1].

card.summary: A stable vitamin A ester used in foods and some skincare; no appearance trials exist.
card.note: Excess preformed vitamin A has documented toxicity.

quick.overview:
Retinyl acetate is a retinol ester used for food fortification, supplements and some anti-aging creams.

No published trial has tested it on skin appearance.
quick.mechanism: It is converted to retinol in the body, which can then be converted to retinoic acid.
quick.risks: As with other vitamin A forms, excess intake can cause hypervitaminosis A. Cosmetic concentrations are capped by EU regulators.
